intro:
2 Samuel is David's reign—the golden era with all its glory and shadows. Opens with David learning of Saul/Jonathan's deaths. He executes the messenger who claimed to kill Saul, sings heartbreaking lament: 'How the mighty have fallen!'

David is anointed king of Judah (southern tribe) at Hebron. Saul's son Ish-bosheth becomes puppet king of Israel (northern tribes) under general Abner. Civil war ensues.

The tide turns when Abner sleeps with Saul's concubine (power move), quarrels with Ish-bosheth, defects to David. David's general Joab murders Abner for killing his brother earlier. David distances himself, mourns publicly: 'Do you not know that a prince has fallen?'

Ish-bosheth is assassinated by his own captains. David executes them for regicide. All tribes come to Hebron: 'We are your bone and flesh.' David becomes king over united Israel at 30.

David captures Jerusalem from Jebusites, makes it capital (neutral territory). Brings ark to Jerusalem with celebration—dancing so hard his wife Michal despises him. God promises David eternal dynasty: 'Your house and kingdom will endure forever' (Davidic Covenant).

Military victories expand borders greater than ever. David shows kindness to Mephibosheth (Jonathan's crippled son), giving him Saul's lands and eating at king's table.

Then the turning point: 'In the spring, when kings go off to war... David remained in Jerusalem.' Sees Bathsheba bathing, sleeps with her (she's married to Uriah the Hittite). She gets pregnant.

David's cover-up spiral: Recalls Uriah from battle, tries to get him to sleep with wife. Uriah refuses while comrades are fighting. David sends him back with death note to Joab: 'Put Uriah in frontline where fighting is fiercest.' Uriah dies. David marries Bathsheba.

Nathan the prophet confronts with parable: Rich man takes poor man's only lamb. David furious: 'That man deserves death!' Nathan: 'YOU are the man!' Consequences: sword will never leave your house, your own household will rebel against you.

Prophesy fulfills immediately: Their baby dies despite David's fasting/prayer.

Then family chaos: David's son Amnon rapes half-sister Tamar. Absalom (Tamar's brother) waits two years, murders Amnon. Absalom flees, returns years later, starts winning people's hearts at city gate. Leads coup, David flees Jerusalem barefoot. Absalom sleeps with David's concubines on palace roof (public power move).

Battle in forest: David orders 'Deal gently with Absalom.' Joab finds Absalom hanging by hair in tree, kills him despite order. David's grief: 'O my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you!'

David returns, deals with more rebellion. Book ends with David's psalms and census sin causing plague. David buys Araunah's threshing floor, builds altar—future temple site.

Through triumph and failure, David remains 'man after God's own heart'—not because perfect, but because he repents deeply and trusts God's covenant.
outro:
2 Samuel closes with David's reign secure but scarred. The final chapters show David's poetic reflections (last words) and his mighty men's exploits. The census plague ends with David's repentance and purchase of Araunah's threshing floor—the exact location where Solomon will build the temple.

Davidic Covenant fulfilled partially: David's line continues, but immediate family experiences the 'sword never departing' consequence. Yet God's mercy remains: Solomon (Bathsheba's second son) will inherit throne.

Key lessons:
1. **Power corrupts** – Even 'man after God's own heart' commits adultery, murder, cover-up when idle and arrogant.
2. **Prophetic confrontation works** – Nathan's parable approach gets through David's defenses where direct accusation might not.
3. **Sin has generational consequences** – David's family becomes a battlefield: rape, murder, rebellion, incest, death.
4. **True repentance** – Psalm 51 (written after Bathsheba) shows raw, honest repentance that God honors.
5. **Leadership legacy** – David's greatest achievement isn't military victories but maintaining heart for God despite epic failures.

Contrast with Saul: David sins worse but repents better. Saul made excuses; David accepted responsibility.

The book shows monarchy's paradox: God establishes David's eternal dynasty while showing how flawed human kings are. This sets up messianic expectation: we need a perfect Davidic king.

1 Kings picks up with David old and dying, succession drama between Adonijah and Solomon. The united kingdom's golden age continues briefly before fracturing.
